title: Volume: Pyramids and Cones

# Volume: Pyramids and Cones

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Understand the one-third relationship between pyramids/cones and prisms/cylinders
- Calculate the volume of a pyramid with any polygonal base
- Calculate the volume of a cone using $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
- Solve problems involving frustums (truncated cones)
- Rearrange the formulas to find missing dimensions

> **Tier:** This topic is **Higher tier** content.

## Introduction

Pyramids and cones come to a point, unlike prisms and cylinders. It turns out that a cone has exactly one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height, and a pyramid has one-third the volume of a prism with the same base and height. This elegant relationship was discovered by ancient Greek mathematicians and is essential for many engineering and architectural calculations.

## Key Concepts

### Volume of a Pyramid

For a pyramid with base area $A$ and vertical height $h$:

$$V = \frac{1}{3} \times A \times h = \frac{1}{3}Ah$$

This works for **any** base shape (square, rectangular, triangular, etc.).

### Volume of a Cone

A cone is a "circular pyramid." For a cone with radius $r$ and vertical height $h$:

$$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$$

> **Key Insight:** The volume of a cone is exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of the volume of a cylinder with the same radius and height.

### Frustum

A **frustum** is formed when the top of a cone or pyramid is cut off by a plane parallel to the base.

$$V_{\text{frustum}} = V_{\text{large cone}} - V_{\text{small cone}}$$

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: Volume of a Square-Based Pyramid
**Question:** A square-based pyramid has a base side of 6 cm and a vertical height of 10 cm. Find the volume.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{base}} &= 6^2 = 36 \text{ cm}^2 \\ V &= \frac{1}{3} \times 36 \times 10 \\ &= \frac{360}{3} \\ &= 120 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

---

### Example 2: Volume of a Cone
**Question:** A cone has radius 7 cm and height 15 cm. Find the volume to 1 decimal place.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h \\ &= \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 7^2 \times 15 \\ &= \frac{1}{3} \times 49\pi \times 15 \\ &= \frac{735\pi}{3} \\ &= 245\pi \\ &= 769.690... \\ &\approx 769.7 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

---

### Example 3: Finding the Height of a Cone
**Question:** A cone has volume $150\pi$ cm$^3$ and radius 5 cm. Find the height.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h \\ 150\pi &= \frac{1}{3}\pi(5)^2 h \\ 150\pi &= \frac{25\pi h}{3} \\ 150 &= \frac{25h}{3} \\ 450 &= 25h \\ h &= 18 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

---

### Example 4: Volume of a Frustum
**Question:** A frustum is formed by removing a small cone of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm from the top of a large cone of radius 9 cm and height 18 cm. Find the volume of the frustum.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{large}} &= \frac{1}{3}\pi(9)^2(18) = \frac{1}{3}\pi(81)(18) = 486\pi \\ V_{\text{small}} &= \frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(6) = \frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(6) = 18\pi \\ V_{\text{frustum}} &= 486\pi - 18\pi = 468\pi \approx 1470.3 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

---

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Forgetting the $\frac{1}{3}$ | Gives triple the correct volume | Always include $\frac{1}{3}$ for pyramids and cones |
| Using slant height instead of vertical height | The volume formula uses vertical height | Use the perpendicular height; use Pythagoras if needed |
| Using diameter instead of radius for cones | The formula uses $r$, not $d$ | Halve the diameter |
| For frustums, subtracting heights instead of volumes | You cannot simply subtract dimensions | Calculate each volume separately, then subtract |

## Summary

- **Pyramid:** $V = \frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times h$
- **Cone:** $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
- Both are exactly $\frac{1}{3}$ of the corresponding prism/cylinder volume.
- **Frustum** = large cone/pyramid volume $-$ small cone/pyramid volume.
- Always use the **vertical height** in these formulas.
